title: JRE 2370 - Dave Smith
guestBio: Dave Smith is a comic, political commentator, host of the "Part of the Problem" podcast, and a co-host of the "Legion of Skanks” podcast.
tldr: Dave Smith makes the libertarian case that American foreign policy interventions generate more instability and enemies than they resolve, using Iraq, Libya, and Syria as evidence of regime change operations that produce the opposite of their stated goals

They debate the non-interventionist position on authoritarian regimes, with Smith arguing most military operations are driven by economic and geopolitical interests rather than genuine humanitarian goals

Drug legalization comes up at length, with Smith connecting prohibition directly to mass incarceration, police militarization, and civil liberties erosion while Joe finds more common ground than expected

Smith distinguishes libertarianism from both mainstream conservatism and progressivism, arguing both major parties engage in authoritarianism in different domains and neither represents genuine opposition to state coercion

Joe and Smith explore the role of comedians in political commentary, with Smith arguing that stand-up culture produces a breed of political thinker who values intellectual honesty over tribal loyalty to either party

The episode closes with discussion of third-party politics and why Smith believes the two-party system structurally prevents meaningful reform on civil liberties and foreign policy no matter which party wins
recap:
Dave Smith is a New York-based stand-up comedian and the host of Part of the Problem, a libertarian-leaning political podcast with a large and devoted following. His JRE appearance gave him a platform to make the libertarian case on a scale few political commentators ever reach, and he used it to challenge some of Joe's assumptions on foreign policy, war, and the role of government.

The conversation opened with Smith laying out the libertarian framework in plain terms: the state is fundamentally coercive, most of its interventions make things worse, and the American foreign policy establishment has a long history of creating the very crises it claims to be solving. Joe, who has spent considerable time talking to people across the political spectrum, pushed back thoughtfully, and the exchange gave Smith room to get specific about the history of US interventions in the Middle East and Latin America.

Foreign policy was the centerpiece of the episode. Smith walked through the logic of non-interventionism, arguing that America's decades of military engagement abroad have generated blowback that creates more enemies than they eliminate. He cited Iraq, Libya, and Syria as case studies in how regime change operations tend to produce destabilization rather than democratic flourishing. Joe challenged Smith on what the alternative looks like when authoritarian regimes commit atrocities, and Smith held firm: most interventions are driven by geopolitical and economic interests, not humanitarian motives.

Drug policy came up as well, with Smith making the straightforward libertarian case for decriminalization or full legalization across the board. They talked about the war on drugs as a government failure, with Smith connecting drug prohibition to mass incarceration, police militarization, and the erosion of civil liberties. Both agreed on more than they might have expected going in, finding common ground on the harms of prohibition even where they differed on solutions.

They also covered comedy and the current state of political discourse, with Smith arguing that the left and right both engage in authoritarian impulses that libertarians find equally troubling. Joe seemed to enjoy the consistency of Smith's framework, even when they disagreed on specific conclusions. Smith made the case that the consistency is the point: a political philosophy that opposes government coercion regardless of which party is doing the coercing is the only honest framework available.

The episode closed on third-party politics, with Smith articulating why he believes neither major party represents a genuine alternative for voters who care about civil liberties and non-interventionism. He made the case for the Libertarian Party as the only vehicle that consistently opposes both warfare and government overreach, and Joe pushed back on the structural barriers to third-party success in American elections without fully dismissing the idea.
